# Discovery of Multiple Light-Harvesting States of the Photosynthetic Protein PE545

# Audrey C. Norris, Catrina Oberg, Leah C. Spangler, Gregory D. Scholes, and Gabriela S. Schlau-Cohen*

Cite This: https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c06307 Read Online

ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * sı Supporting Information

ABSTRACT: Cryptophytes are photosynthetic microalga that flourish in a remarkable diversity of natural environments by using pigment-containing proteins with absorption maxima tuned to each ecological niche. While this diversity in the absorption has been well established, the subsequent photophysics is highly sensitive to the local protein environment and so may exhibit similar variation. Thermal fluctuations of the protein conformation are expected to introduce photophysical heterogeneity of the pigments that may have evolved important functional properties in a manner similar to that of the absorption. However, such heterogeneity is averaged out in ensemble measurements and, therefore, has not yet been probed. Here, we report single-molecule measurements of phycoerythrin 545 (PE545), the prototypical cryptophyte antenna protein, in its native dimeric form. A conformational ensemble was resolved consisting of distinct photophysical states with different light-harvesting properties. Proteins that did not quench, partially quenched, or fully quenched absorbed light were observed. Light intensity increased the quenchedstate population of the dimer, potentially as a mechanism to deal with the extreme light intensities found in aqueous environments. Cross-linking, which mimics local interactions, introduces this light-dependent functionality while also suppressing other conformational dynamics. The cellular organization can, therefore, actively modulate the protein conformation and dynamics, selecting for distinct levels of light harvesting. Thus, the complex conformational equilibrium provides an additional mechanism for cryptophytes and likely other photosynthetic organisms to optimize solar energy capture and conversion. ■INTRODUCTION Cryptophytes are aquatic algae that are found in diverse environments. Key to their survival under different conditions is their unique and tunable light-harvesting machinery.1,2

Unlike all other known photosynthetic species, the primary light-harvesting proteins have no higher-order organization but instead are densely packed within the thylakoid lumen. For other species, changes to the higher-order organization modulate light harvesting in response to changes in the growth conditions. For cryptophytes, the lack of organization means that light harvesting must be modulated within the light-harvesting proteins themselves. While it has been shown that different light conditions can lead to the expression of up to 20 different protein sequences, no associated differences in their absorption or energy transfer properties have been observed.3−5 Studies of cryptophyte light-harvesting proteins in their native dimeric configuration have been limited to ensemble measurements, which are averaged over such differences. Here, we use single-molecule measurements to resolve individual dimers with different photophysical properties, which may serve as distinct functional states for robust light harvesting in vivo. The photosynthetic machinery of cryptophytes efficiently captures both the bluer wavelength light present underwater as

well as any available longer wavelength light.6 Cryptophytes contain two light-harvesting systems tuned to these two spectral regions: membrane-intrinsic light-harvesting complexes with chlorophyll as the main photopigment that surround the reaction center2,7 and phycobiliproteins that act as their primary photoreceptors.2,6−9 Phycobiliproteins are most abundant in cyanobacteria and red algae, in which multiple types of phycobiliproteins are organized into higherorder stacking structures, most notably the phycobilisome.10 In contrast, in cryptophytes, only one type of phycobiliprotein is found in each species and is organized in a dense layer within the thylakoid lumen with no known order.2,7,8,11−13 Both their structure and organization of phycobiliproteins is unique among known species, yet can still maintain extremely high light-harvesting efficiency, indicating that energy transfer

Phycobiliproteins are constructed from (αβ) monomeric subunit. The β subunits are highly conserved among species, but the α components are specific to species, and each species can express different versions of these subunits depending on light conditions.3−5,17 While many oligomeric states have been observed in cyanobacteria and red algae, the phycobiliproteins exist solely as heterodimers of the monomeric subunits in cryptophytes. In these organisms, the spectral properties are widely tunable based on pigment identity, number, organization, and interactions with the protein scaffold specific to species and growth conditions.2,14,18−20 The pigment identity can also reversibly be changed in response to the environment, shifting the absorption based on light levels.21 The most wellstudied cryptophyte phycobiliprotein is the light-harvesting complex phycoerythrin 545 (PE545). PE545 is a heterodimer with identical β subunits sandwiching the slightly different α subunits (Figure 1a). The main difference between the two α subunits in the 1XG0 structure shown in Figure 1a is the fact that the α1 subunit is 5 amino acids longer than the α2 subunit. PE545 dimers contain eight covalently bound pigments, three phycoerythrobilins (PEB) in each β subunit, and one dihydrobiliverdin (DBV) in each α subunit.22−24 The two PEB pigments positioned at the monomer−monomer interface couple strongly to form dimeric electronic states that funnel energy outward to the lower energy DBV pigment that serves as the emitter.13,23−25 The protein scaffold undergoes conformational fluctuations due to thermal motion that are expected to impact the electronic properties and dynamics of these pigments. However, studies of the electronic structure

and dynamics have been at the ensemble level, which averages these conformations. Single-molecule methods were developed to uncover such underlying distributions, which exposes the link between conformations and photophysical properties.26−32

For phycobiliproteins from cyanobacteria and red algae, such distributions have been extensively studied, revealing how the conformational state of the protein scaffold can induce spectrally distinct states and how the various pigments create specific quenching pathways.33,34 For phycobiliproteins from cryptophytes, monomeric PE545 has been investigated,35 and quenched conformations were observed with rapid dynamics between them. While the presence of an equilibrium involving quenched conformations was established in this study, the role of these conformations in cellular function remained unclear. In particular, conformational states are highly sensitive to the local environment, including oligomerization. Thus, investigations of the functional role of these conformational states require the native dimeric form and parameters that mimic the cellular environment, neither of which have been examined. The conformational states of PE545 in its native dimeric form and their associated functional differences have not been investigated. Here, we report single-molecule measurements of dimeric PE545 from the Rhodomonas minuta strain CPCC344. Three conformational states with distinct fluorescence lifetimes were observed, reflecting different levels of excited-state quenching. For cross-linked dimeric PE545, the quenched states increased with light intensity, providing photoprotective functionality. Remarkably, the dimer is the native form, and cross-linking can mimic the structural constraints due to interactions in the densely packed lumenal space, so the discovery of behaviors

Subpopulations with different access to the three states were identified, most notably for the cross-linked proteins, revealing differences in the lightharvesting properties between individual proteins in the presence of structural constraints. The functional differences between individual dimeric PE545 proteins may therefore be modulated by the lumenal environment. Such protein-level behaviors are potentially a mechanism utilized by cryptophytes to flourish in a wide range of environments and conditions, despite the disordered and immobile architecture of their lightharvesting systems.36,37 ■RESULTS

PE545 Cross-Linking and Characterization. Dimeric PE545 was stabilized by developing a cross-linking protocol. Phycobiliproteins dissociate into monomers at low concentrations, such as those required for single-molecule measurements.38−40 While robust lysine cross-linking protocols are well established for cyanobacterial phycobiliproteins,41 PE545 has fewer lysines, so the protocol was modified to use a longer spacing arm to adjust for the sparsity of the residues. The cross-linked PE545 sample was then separated into both purified monomers or dimers. Successful production and isolation of each oligomeric form (≥90% band percentage) was confirmed with SDS-PAGE, shown in Figure 1b. The ensemble absorbance and emission spectra of non-cross-linked monomeric PE545, cross-linked monomeric PE545, and cross-linked dimeric PE545 are overlaid along with the 545 nm laser emission in Figure 1c. The cross-linked samples display similar spectral profiles to the non-cross-linked one, showing the overall integrity of PE545 is maintained. Ensemble fluorescence lifetime measurements were also performed for all samples (Figure 1d) and were well fit with monoexponential decay (Table S3). The fluorescence lifetimes of the non-cross-

linked monomer and the cross-linked dimer were ∼2.6 ns, whereas the lifetime of the cross-linked monomer decreased to 2.1 ns. The shortening of the lifetime exclusively in the cross-linked monomer may arise from a structural perturbation at the monomer−monomer interface. Thirteen of the 18 total lysines in the monomerwhen linked with BS(PEG)9span an area at least partially covering the scaffold on the monomer− monomer interface (Figures S8 and S9). At this interface, the central PEB pigment is fairly surface exposed, and so any modifications or restrictions in the protein scaffold at this interface will likely directly impact this pigment. In particular, three solvent accessible lysines (two on the β subunit and one on the α subunit) are extremely close to this central pigment, making them likely candidates for the observed lifetime perturbation and illustrating that surrounding structural perturbations can impact the photophysics. Single-Molecule Fluorescence Intensity and Lifetime. Single-molecule spectroscopy can resolve distinct photophysical states, which report on different functional subpopulations.42 To determine these states as well as the underlying protein conformations and dynamics, we performed single-molecule measurements on three PE545 samples (Figure 2). Representative single-molecule fluorescence traces are shown in Figure 2b for the first 400 s of observation to visualize the single-molecule behavior prior to photodegradation. Full traces are shown in Figure S1. All three traces show indicators of a single emitter, including blinking and single-step photobleaching. Different photophysical states, distinguished by differences in the intensity or lifetime, are clearly present. The photophysics of the embedded pigments is highly sensitive to the surrounding protein conformation, so the different states are typically ascribed to conformations of the antenna protein.

To determine the distribution of photophysical states, the fluorescence intensity and corresponding lifetime for all levels of all molecules in that sample accessed were combined to generate density plots (Figure 2c). For example, the top density plot in Figure 2c shows all levels that all non-crosslinked monomer molecules accessed. Lifetime decay traces could not be fit for levels with less than 500 signal photons, so these levels were excluded from these plots and further analysis. Low-intensity states with lifetimes below the instrument response function threshold (∼450 ps) were denoted as “Off”. The remaining set of lifetime values exhibited a broad distribution for all samples without any clear clustering. Broad distributions are typically observed for single-molecule measurements with dependence on the sample and the local environment.43−45 The breadth can arise from several molecular factors, including small structural heterogeneity between the individual proteins, differences in the local interactions with the polymer matrix, and experimental fluctuations in the collected photon stream. For the total intensity distributions, the median was 129 counts per 100 ms (cnts/100 ms) for the non-cross-linked monomer, 121 cnts/100 ms for the cross-linked monomer, and 114 cnts/100 ms for the cross-linked dimer, which together reflects a fluorescence intensity decrease upon cross-linking and dimerization. For the monomer samples, the reduction upon cross-linking originates from the lower population with fluorescence intensities above 350 cnts/100 ms with no population above 900 cnts/100 ms for the cross-linked monomer (Figure S3). For the cross-linked samples, the reduction upon dimerization originates from the nearly total redistribution into the population with fluorescence intensities below 100 cnts/100 ms. For the intensity distribution of the fluorescence immediately upon illumination (Figure S3b), which reflects the nonphotodegraded behavior, these trends were observed with larger differences. The median intensity was 326 cnts/100 ms for the non-cross-linked monomer, 241 cnts/100 ms for the cross-linked monomer, and 313 cnts/100 ms for the cross-linked dimer. The intensity decrease upon cross-linking suggests that the structural constraints may compress the protein to induce rapid quenching channels and/or change the radiative and nonradiative rates. However,

limited mechanistic information can be determined from the intensity values alone. For the total lifetime distributions, the values for all levels were used to construct the one-dimensional histograms that more clearly visualize underlying behaviors, Figure 1d. In contrast to the intensity, similar lifetime distributions were observed for the cross-linked and non-cross-linked monomers with nearly identical medians of 1.90 and 1.91 ns, respectively. Furthermore, a clear reduction to a median of only 1.55 ns was observed upon dimerization. Likely, the low state in the monomer can quench the other protomer, generating an increase in the quenched population for the dimer sample. To resolve the underlying lifetime states, which typically arise from distinct protein conformations,26 an inverse Laplace transform (ILT) was performed on the single-molecule data. An inverse Laplace transform is a mathematical model that converts an exponential decay into a distribution of decay values, i.e., a distribution in τ-space. The τ-space distributions for all three samples are overlaid on top of the one-dimensional lifetime histograms in Figure 2d. Two peaks, or lifetime states, were present in all the τ-space distribution at ∼2.5 and ∼1 ns, denoted “high” and “low”, respectively. The specific maxima for each sample are reported in Table S4 and are indicated with dashed lines. The two lifetime states are well separated by a division at 1.5 ns, which is also indicated in the density plots in Figure 2c. The similar values in all three samples indicate that the same states, i.e., conformations, are populated upon cross-linking and upon dimerization. The relative amplitudes of the lifetime states, calculated through the peak areas, correspond to their photon-weighted populations. The amplitude of the high state was similar at 75% for the noncross-linked monomer and 71% for the cross-linked monomer, indicating relative populations do not change with crosslinking. In contrast, the high-state amplitude decreased to 59% for the cross-linked dimer. The decrease in high-state population upon dimerization is quantitatively consistent with a model where one monomer within a dimer can quench the other protomer, as described above. Overall, the same lifetime states, or conformations, are retained, but the conformational ensemble of functional states is altered through oligomerization.

State Switching Kinetics. The conformational and photophysical dynamics of PE545 can be observed through the switches between distinct intensity levels. The time between switches is termed the dwell time. To capture the overall dynamics for each data set, the dwell time histogram for all levels was fit to an exponential decay to determine the average switching rate, ⟨ktot⟩(Figures 3a, and S12). The total switching rates were 0.48 s−1 for the non-cross-linked monomer, 0.23 s−1 for the cross-linked monomer, and 0.31 s−1 for the cross-linked dimer. The rate decrease upon crosslinking is consistent with previous work on phycobiliproteins from cyanobacteria.41 The rate increase upon dimerization suggests that transitions in either monomer can impact the fluorescence of the dimer, in line with the results from the state distributions, where an increased quenched population was observed in the dimer. Three main avenues exist to switch between the identified fluorescence states and so contribute to the total switching rate: conformational dynamics, which are transitions between high and low lifetime states; blinking, which is transiently entering a nonemissive, or ”Off”, fluorescence state; and photobleaching, which is the irreversible photoinduced destruction of an individual pigment that decreases the intensity owing to the decrease in number of photoactive

pigments. The rates for each avenue were calculated from their branching ratios and the total switching rate (SI Section 4). In order to characterize the power dependence of the three avenues, single-molecule experiments were performed at two fluences, 100 and 310 nJ/cm2. For photobleaching, the behavior was consistent with previous work on phycobiliproteins35 (Figures S11−S13). For conformational dynamics and blinking, the extracted rates for the cross-linked monomer and dimer are plotted in Figure 3b for both laser fluences. The photon dependence for each rate was determined by fitting the values at both powers to a linear function. When the rate increases with increasing fluence, the process responsible for the transition is photoinduced due to either the available photon energy overcoming an activation barrier or an evolution from the excited state. Conversely, when the rate showed minimal fluence dependence, the process was thermal in nature. The relative rates and state populations at both fluences were visualized in Figure 3c for the cross-linked dimer. Conformational dynamics, the transitions between high and low states, is the slowest process with predominantly thermal rates. This aligns well with the biological picture of a protein scaffold rearrangement, ultimately being responsible for these transitions, which is a part of the natural behavior of the antenna protein. Blinking, the transient transition into the off state, is generally a faster process again with predominantly thermal rates. The underlying mechanism for many of these transitions may also be a protein scaffold rearrangement. The exception is the on-to-off rate again for the cross-linked dimer, which is photoinduced with an increase by a factor of 1.49. In this case, when the antenna protein molecules are exposed to high light, the off-state population increases only minimally because of the fast transition rate back to the on state, which rapidly depletes the population of the off state. Overall, the presence of thermal processes indicates that fluctuations in the protein generate heterogeneity in the photophysical properties. A notable exception is the presence of photoinduced transitions into the low and off states only observed for the dimer, whereas only thermal transitions are present for the monomer. Under high light conditions, therefore, the quenched-state populations increase in this physiological oligomer, potentially with a photoprotective function. Lifetime State Subpopulations. Single-molecule measurements reveal two key properties: asynchronous dynamics, such as the protein fluctuations described above, and heterogeneity. Examination of the individual molecules revealed three subpopulations with distinct fluorescence lifetime distributions (Figure 4 and Table S1): Type I (Figure 4a, left), which accessed predominately the high state (≥90%) of the observation time; Type II (Figure 4a, middle), which accessed both high and low lifetime states; and Type III (Figure 4a, right), which predominantly accessed the low lifetime state. Example traces for each type are shown in Figure 4a. Every molecule from each data set was classified into one of the three types, resulting in lifetime distributions. The distributions are color-coordinated with the columns in Figure 4a, with a cartoon representation in Figure 4b highlighting which row of the distributions corresponds to which data set. The Type I subpopulation is present in all samples at ∼20% of the molecules. The Type II subpopulation dominates all samples at 74, 57, and 66% for the non-cross-linked monomer, cross-linked monomer, and cross-linked dimer, respectively. The Type III subpopulation was found exclusively in the crosslinked samples at 9 and 20% for the monomer and dimer, respectively. The ILT distribution for each subpopulation is also overlaid on the lifetime distributions from the intensity levels. These show the expected redistribution where the high lifetime state dominates in Type I, the low lifetime state in Type III, and both states are present in Type II. Minor populations of the low and high lifetime states for Type I and Type III, respectively, likely indicate preferential access to their predominant state rather than complete trapping. These subpopulations were present in different ratios for each sample. Pie charts in Figure 4c illustrate the subpopulation distributions for each sample. A comparison of the two monomer samples shows that cross-linking introduced a substantial increase in molecules that preferentially access only one of the lifetime states (Type I, Type III), consistent with the reduction in dynamics. The number of Type I and Type III molecules increased nearly equivalently (Figure 4a,c), which is responsible for the similar lifetime distributions of the non-cross-linked and cross-linked monomers.

Comparison of the cross-linked monomer to the crosslinked dimer shows that dimerization shifted the population from Type I to Type III. As discussed above, a single monomer likely acts as a quencher for the entire dimer, leading to an overall increase in the low-state population. The predicted probability of either monomer within the dimer being Type III is 17%, closely matching the experimental value of 20%. Overall, the observation and resolution of the Type I, II, and III subpopulations reveals that the ensemble of PE545 contains heterogeneous individual proteins influenced by both crosslinking and dimerization. These factors suggest an underlying structural origin of the heterogeneity, which in turn gives rise to distinct light-harvesting states. ■DISCUSSION PE545 is found within a dense uniform layer in the thylakoid lumen. The phycobiliprotein content increases further under low light conditions,46,47 suggesting that an extremely high density can be reached. As a result, the phycobiliproteins are constricted in mobility within the lumenal space,36,37,48 likely limiting access for reorganization, repair, and/or replacement. Distinct functional states thus must be encoded into the protein structure itself, with modulation of the structure by passive factors such as density and oligomerization rather than requiring active machinery that cannot easily reorganize the disordered lumenal space. Here, we report a complex conformational equilibrium of PE545 with three functional states with distinct levels of quenching. The cross-linked dimer most closely mimics the native condition, as it is both the physiological oligomer and the cross-linking can capture the structural constraints within the cellular environment. For the dimer alone, the transitions between the states exhibit a fluence dependence that suggests many are present at physiological light conditions, indicating that dynamic and fluctuating behaviors underlie ensemble measurements. Thus, the multiplicity of conformational states observed for PE545 may enable robust functionality without the need to access the lightharvesting protein machinery. Notably, subpopulations are also present for the cross-linked dimers and are distinguished by distinct equilibria between the functional states. Such protein-level heterogeneity reflects intrinsic differences, potentially induced by the variations in protein sequence that have been associated with growth conditions.3−5 While such genotypic variation was established previously, the resultant phenotypic variation had not been determined. The reported single-molecule results represent the first evidence of a potential functional outcome. In oxygenic photosynthesis, a set of photoprotective processes, known as nonphotochemical quenching (NPQ),2

occur under high light conditions. In cryptophytes, NPQ has only been identified in the membrane-intrinsic light-harvesting complexes49−53 with no such processes yet observed in the phycobiliproteins.51−53 In contrast, in the homologous phycobiliproteins from red algae and cyanobacteria, photoprotective processes induced by regulatory proteins have been identified.54 In these organisms, the phycobiliproteins are easily accessed by other proteins and/or replaced when damaged, unlike in cryptophytes. Cryptophytes therefore need a noninvasive way to conserve their phycobiliproteins proteins under high light. Cryptophytes may prevent photodamage by leveraging the low and off states to safely dissipate excess energy, analogous to the fastest component (qE) of NPQ in green plants. The mechanism for energy dissipation is

unknown. We speculate that it might involve a radiationless deactivation of the excited state by the photoisomerization of bilin molecules, with a thermal reversal in the ground state. The thermal nature of the return to the high/on states suggests that the transition corresponds to a photoinduced rearrangement of the surrounding protein scaffold, and so the protein may have evolved such functionality. The lack of traditional NPQ pathways in the phycobiliproteins of cryptophytes indicates that in vivo PE545 likely uses an alternative mechanism such as controlling the protein conformational equilibrium as observed here. ■CONCLUSIONS The complex conformational landscape of PE545 reveals distinct functional states, transitions between them, and heterogeneous subpopulations within the ensemble of proteins. High light shifts the protein conformational equilibrium into the quenched states for dimeric PE545, indicating the possibility that the scaffold itself has a photoprotective functionality in the native form. The discovery of phenotypic diversity primarily through the subpopulations, potentially encoded by genotypic diversity, reveals a previously unappreciated flexibility in the functional properties of the light-harvesting apparatus. Collectively, these properties of the protein scaffold of PE545 may enable flexible and responsive light harvesting for cryptophytes despite the highly restricted organization of their phycobiliproteins, allowing these organisms to flourish across diverse aquatic environments. ■METHODS

Sample Preparation and Purification. Algae growth and phycobiliprotein purification followed established protocols.22,55

Briefly, cryptophyte species R. minuta strain CPCC344 was grown in CHU-10 media under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle. To isolate and purify the antenna complex PE545, the cells were exposed to a freeze/ thaw cycle and multiple ammonium sulfate precipitations of 40, 55, and 80%. The phycobiliprotein subunits were then collected via a 25 min ultracentrifugation at 35,000g, and dialysis against 25 mM phosphate buffer at 6.5 pH removed any residual ammonium sulfate. The purified PE545 samples were stored at −80 °C. The frozen solutions were thawed on ice (∼0 °C) and diluted to the required concentrations using a 25 mM phosphate buffer at pH 6.6. Cross-Linking Protocol. Cross-linking (XL) was performed by reacting the sulfo-NHS ester groups PEGylated bis (sulfosuccinimidyl) suberate) (BS(PEG)9, ThermoFisher Scientific) with primary amines on PE545. The reactions were incubated at room temperature and quenched with 3 M Tris (pH 7.5) (Sigma-Aldrich). The crosslinked dimers were purified with FPLC using a size-exclusion column (Superdex 75 Increase 10/300 GL) and stored at 4 °C. The procedure was optimized for each PE545 purification individually because differences in growth conditions can modify which α-subunits are expressed.3−5 The BS(PEG)9 to PE545 ratio was varied from 100- to 3000-fold, and maximum dimer formation was identified by SDS- PAGE. Protein integrity was confirmed by fluorescence-correlation spectroscopy (FCS) before and after the single-molecule experiments (Figure S7a). Ensemble Measurements. All steady-state measurements were performed with ∼200 μL of the PE545 sample in a quartz 10 × 2 mm2 cuvette. The steady-state fluorescence spectra were measured with a Varian Cary Eclipse (∼2 nW), and the absorbance spectra were measured with an Agilent Cary 5000 spectrometer (≤20 au lamp energy). Fluorescence-correlation spectroscopy (FCS) measurements were conducted using the home-built confocal setup described in the following section, with coverslips containing roughly 60 μL of 50−400 nM solutions depending on the sample, and an excitation of 1.5 nW. Ensemble fluorescence lifetimes were measured using a Spectra

Physics Mai Tai Ti:sapphire laser. The desired excitation of 545 nm (1−7 μW) was filtered from a broadband range (430−1000 nm) using a band-pass filter (ET550/15x, Chroma). Further details can be found in the SI.

Single-Molecule Measurements. PE545 was diluted down to 500 pM-2 nM in a 25 mM 6.6 pH phosphate buffer. 60 μL of the diluted solution containing 1% poly(vinyl alcohol) and the enzymatic oxygen scavenger system of 50 nM pyranose oxidase (Sigma-Aldrich), 100 nM catalase (Sigma-Aldrich) and 5 mM glucose (Sigma-Aldrich) was spin-coated onto a glass coverslip resulting in roughly one molecule every square micron. Single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy experiments were conducted on a home-built confocal microscope using a 545 nm excitation laser (FemtoFiber pro, Toptica; 130 fs pulse duration, 80 MHz repetition rate) with a power of 8.6 and 26 nW on the sample plane for the low and high fluence measurements, respectively. This corresponds to an energy density of approximately 100 and 310 nJ/ cm2. The excitation laser was focused onto the sample plane using an objective (UPLSAPO100XO, Olympus, NA 1.4), and fluorescence was collected through the same objective, separated by a dichroic mirror (ZT568rdc-UF3, Chroma) and emission filter (FF01−600/ 52−25, Semrock), and detected with an avalanche photodiode (SPCM-AQRH-15, Excelitas). Photon arrival times were recorded by using a time-correlated single-photon counting device (Time- Tagger20, Swabian Instruments). The instrument response function (IRF) was measured using scattered light at 450 ps full width at halfmaximum. Sample sizes were 156, 129, and 235 antenna complexes for the non-cross-linked monomer, cross-linked monomer, and crosslinked dimer, respectively. Single-Molecule Data Analysis. The photon stream was binned into 100 ms intervals. A change-point algorithm56 was applied to determine the emission intensity levels for each complex. The times between excitation and emission were histogrammed for each level, and the resulting decay curves were fit to extract the fluorescence lifetimes. Representative fit curves are shown in the SI (Figure S1b). A kernel density estimation algorithm from Matlab was applied to the intensity and corresponding lifetime values to generate a twodimensional plot. The algorithm generates a two-dimensional probability density plot from the distribution using a Gaussian smoothing function and a default bandwidth that should optimally capture a normal distribution. A one-dimensional inverse Laplace transformation (1D-ILT) algorithm57 was implemented to extract the lifetime distribution in a model-free manner. The program developed in the group converts the fluorescence decay signal from the experimental time axis into the lifetime axis, which allows the direct extraction of the lifetime distribution. A more thorough explanation is located in the SI. The dynamics of the samples were determined by extracting the transition rates between the three different identified fluorescence states: High (τ ≥1.5 ns), Low (1.5 ns ≥τ ≥0.55 ns), and Off (0.55 ns ≥τ). An average switching rate, ⟨ktot⟩, was determined by fitting the dwell time histogram to a two-component exponential decay and averaging the components. The total rate is equivalent to the sum of all of the individual switching rates between the different lifetime states. The individual switching rates were therefore calculated by using a branching method. The total dwell time in each state was determined along with the number of events for a certain behavior, and the ratio was calculated. This is explained in further detail in the SI in Section 4. Single-Molecule Subpopulation Classification. Each singlemolecule trace was classified into three possible subpopulations using a lifetime cutoff of 1.5 ns. Traces that spent the majority of their time (≥90% of all lifetime levels) in fluorescence lifetime states above that cutoff were classified as Type I, and those that spent the majority below that cutoff were classified as Type III. Traces that did not show a dramatic preference for the High vs Low lifetime state were labeled Type II. Three representative traces from the cross-linked dimer data set are shown in Figure 4a.
